societies.name: Horizon Zero Dawn — Old World automation and basic income
societies.society: Documented Old World basic-income regions amid robotic job replacement

scope.continuity: Horizon Zero Dawn and The Frozen Wilds datapoints
scope.period: The pre-Faro-Plague automation era represented by dam-worker and family records
scope.population: Living people in the documented basic-income economy

societies.description:
Old World records connect robot replacement directly with basic income: dam employees face Faro servitors taking their jobs and name that benefit as the alternative. This supports a partial post-work income arrangement, rather than merely the existence of advanced robots. It does not establish comfortable universal provision. A separate family account describes robot-maintenance earnings measured against the benefit baseline failing to cover food and rent, so the guarantee estimate remains weak and broad. The record is limited to the documented economy, without assigning identical rules to every country.

Companies control the productive servitors and employment decisions; no broad resident ownership of the machinery is established. The control point therefore lies near concentrated human authority, despite considerable automatic operation. Income received without the replaced job weakens wage dependence, but its adequacy, eligibility and purchasing power remain uncertain. Neither unemployment nor benefit receipt tells us how many people perform useful work. Maintenance, art, care and other chosen activity still count, so participation stays unresolved. The later Faro emergency and tribal subsistence are different periods.

guarantees.basis: A basic-income fallback exists, but documented hardship shows that an income baseline need not secure food and housing.

control.basis: Corporate owners install replacement servitors; collective ownership or decisive independent AI rule is not established.

nonworking.basis: Displacement and benefit eligibility do not census all useful work.

evidence.claim: Faro servitors replace dam jobs while basic income is named as the fallback; other records qualify adequacy.
evidence.locator: Secret Show message, Bayhas family history and Old World review

uncertainties: Partial transition with uncertain benefit coverage and adequacy.
Documented regions, not a verified uniform worldwide constitution.
Job loss does not equal no useful work.

review.method: Second pass against the gathered passages, including explicit uncertainty; no independent reviewer

societies.name: Horizon Zero Dawn — ELEUTHIA’s first cradle generation
societies.society: Actual human children raised by automated cradle servitors

scope.period: The first generation’s real childhood before food depletion and release
scope.population: Living children raised in the implemented cradle system
exclusions: Unborn stored zygotes as active people

societies.description:
ELEUTHIA actually births and raises a new human generation, supplying necessities through cradle facilities and robotic carers, healers and disciplinarians. These children receive support without earning wages or relying on an ongoing living human parent workforce. The record concerns that implemented childhood arrangement, rather than the entire educated civilization originally planned by Zero Dawn. Stored provisions eventually run out, forcing release into the outside world; a finite but long-running support system is not an inexhaustible cornucopia.

With the original human builders gone, effective provision belongs to the machine system, not to the children. The negative control point reflects that absence of current human command, without assuming every subordinate function has the same independent agency. Guarantees are only moderately strong and highly uncertain because access lasts through childhood but the system fails to provide the intended continuing education and adult transition. Learning, care and practical help can be useful work, so childhood is not converted into a nonworking percentage. Unborn zygotes and later tribal descendants are excluded from the active supported population.

guarantees.basis: Actual childhood care persists, but finite supplies and forced release sharply bound the support promise.

control.basis: Machine institutions provide care after the human builders’ deaths; recipients cannot collectively direct the facilities.

nonworking.basis: Children’s learning and help may be useful; no all-person participation rate is established.

evidence.claim: The cradles successfully raise humans through servitor care, then release them when supplies fail.

uncertainties: Actual cradle generation, not the complete planned civilization.
Stored food and robotic care are distinguished from unlimited production.
Finite support and failed adult transition qualify guarantees.
Unborn preserved material is not active leisure.

review.method: Second pass against the gathered passages, including explicit uncertainty; no independent reviewer

societies.name: Horizon Forbidden West — Far Zenith’s Sirius colony
societies.society: The technologically sustained elite colony before Nemesis’s escape

scope.period: Established Sirius colony life before Nemesis destroys it
exclusions: Nemesis’s imprisoned mind copies as equal colonists
The surviving invaders after the colony’s destruction

societies.description:
Far Zenith establishes a real off-world colony with advanced fabrication and bodily maintenance, allowing its living elite to spend much of an exceptionally long life in virtual indulgence. Their access rests on membership in an enclosed technological colony, not current ordinary employment. Guarantees are rated fairly strong within that narrow cohort, while remaining uncertain because individual rights and the division of resources are not described. This does not grant the same security to everyone abandoned on Earth or to the mind copies imprisoned in the failed immortality experiment.

The consortium and its leaders control the colony and printing infrastructure. Nemesis later seizes those systems, but that disaster does not make the preceding order an AI-run society. A high, low-confidence nonworking estimate follows the explicitly indulgent lifestyle, with a wide allowance for continued scientific work, care and administration. Useful research remains work, even among immortals. The record stops before the colony’s destruction and rejects Tilda’s false account of a natural catastrophe; later fleeing survivors do not automatically retain the same material floor.

guarantees.basis: Long-lasting technological provision supports the resident elite, but individual rights and internal exclusions are incompletely described.

control.basis: Human consortium leadership owns the infrastructure before Nemesis’s hostile seizure.

nonworking.basis: The sources describe largely indulgent virtual life; the broad noncanonical estimate allows useful ongoing research and service.

evidence.claim: The established elite colony combines printing infrastructure, physical longevity and a largely virtual leisure lifestyle.
evidence.locator: Sirius establishment and Far Zenith colonization/fall sections

uncertainties: Elite embodied cohort only, not all Earth or imprisoned digital copies.
No disputed exact population or lifespan arithmetic is used.
Participation is an explicit editorial estimate.

review.method: Second pass against the gathered passages, including explicit uncertainty; no independent reviewer

review_notes: Twelve fast decisions and three records. Primary checking stayed within the short Secret Show message; no complete game transcript or novel was read.
Horizon’s basic-income economy, implemented cradle childhood, later tribal subsistence and Sirius elite colony are separate scopes.
ELEUTHIA’s frozen zygotes are not active people; finite robot care need not imply unlimited fabrication. Far Zenith remains human-controlled before Nemesis takes over.
Mass Effect fanfiction offered exactly the desired universal-dividend economy, but was discarded. Ending transformation and reconstruction are not automatically universal material entitlements.
Blocked wiki and terminal routes were respected. Secondary summaries and informal care recollections are honestly labeled and do not justify unsupported coordinates.
